Had the same problem with the pulley being hard to place on the shaft. Since the shaft itself has some play in the motor, here is what I did: took one of the M3x6 screws I just released, paled it into one of the holes of the frame (head upwards). The you can place the shaft on the screw had so it cannot move anymore. Use one hand to hold the motor and the spacer, and with the other hand you can then press on the pulley without risking to break the motor.

As a caution, I had a hard time getting the pulleys on my MK4 motors, as several mentioned. Because of this I didn’t push the pulley on the left side down enough on the shaft and it was causing all kinds of calibration issues. Fixed it now, but that meant taking the left side panel off to get access to the motor again and thus all the spool holders on that side had to come off. I’m planning on using dry boxes, so I think I will just skip putting the spool holders back on that side. If I really need a spool holder, I can use them on 5-8, still. But someone really should take a look at this shaft issue.
Check the set screws in your new pulley. The set screws protruded slightly into the interior. I loosened mine slightly and the pulley slid right on to the shaft, no problem.

Several comments have raised the issue of the motor pulleys being too small (regarding their inner diameter—ID). My pulleys were equally stubborn when I first attempted to put them on. Before using some extra uggah-buggah to get them on, I stopped and took some measurements. In my case, the pulley IDs measured 5.01mm and the motor shafts measured 4.97mm. There’s only 0.04mm clearance between them—that ain’t much! This means the surfaces of the motor shafts and the bores of the pulleys need to be PERFECT in order for them to slide on smoothly. However, they’re not. The cup-point grub screws cut into the shafts, leaving burrs, and the hole and thread cutting (for the grub screws) into the pulley bore also leaves burrs. I used the edges of the flutes on a 3/16” (~4.76mm) drill bit to deburr the bores (manually!—rotating the bit between my fingers—do not use a power tool for this!) on the pulleys and followed that up by wrapping a piece of 2000 grit sandpaper over the shank of the drill bit and making another pass inside the bore with that. I used the same 2000 grit sandpaper to clean up the motor shafts. Back out the grub screws or remove them completely before deburring the bores on the pulleys. Once I did all of this, my pulleys slid onto the motor shafts easily.

There is a helpful picture in step #21 of how the belts operate in a few steps that would be more useful as 8.5 since it shows the concept.  The right motor here in step 9 drives the lower belt, the upper belt is driven by the left motor, so the drive gears are offset. The left side pulley will go on the opposite way and use the other side of the tool, so just leaving that note back here to warn you from blasting through and doing it the same (wrong for that side) way.
